sceneAlt: A quiet pool scene study with a horse-shaped figure floating in blue water
artAlt: A study of David Hockney's Portrait of an Artist with two figures by a pool
title: Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)
museum: Private collection (sold at Christie's, New York, 2018)
choices: David Hockney · Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)
reveal: The painting above BoJack's desk echoes Hockney's cool pool, distant swimmer, and bright California light.
sceneNote: A glossy self-portrait becomes a quietly brutal picture of watching someone drift away. The pool is a stage, and BoJack is always both actor and audience.
artFact: Hockney painted this after the end of a long relationship, using the pool's surface to hold two people in the same frame while keeping them emotionally apart.

sceneAlt: A red-room scene study with five simplified figures moving in a circle
artAlt: A study of Henri Matisse's dance paintings with five red figures
title: The Dance / Dance (II) (attribution varies)
reveal: A wall in the early episodes turns Matisse's linked dancers into a wry, animal-party loop. Published references disagree on whether the match is The Dance (1910) or Dance (II) (1932), so this round keeps both readings visible.
sceneNote: The reference keeps the original's radical simplicity: bodies become a rhythm, a circle becomes a room, and the background does the emotional heavy lifting.
artFact: Matisse reduced the figures to a handful of sweeping contours so the painting reads as movement before it reads as anatomy.

sceneAlt: A pop-art scene study showing three bright, repeating shoe silhouettes
artAlt: A study of Andy Warhol's Diamond Dust Shoes with repeated silver shoes
title: Diamond Dust Shoes
reveal: The show borrows Warhol's repetition and sparkle for a trio of pop-art shoes that look glamorous, disposable, and a little sad.
sceneNote: It is a joke about celebrity objects: the shoes are instantly legible as status, then instantly empty once the shine wears off.
artFact: Warhol used crushed glass particles, or diamond dust, to make the surface catch light like a product display.

sceneAlt: A gold-patterned scene study with two simplified figures inside a tall frame
artAlt: A study of Gustav Klimt's The Kiss with gold geometric patterns
title: The Kiss
reveal: Klimt's gold embrace gets a Hollywoo makeover: the pattern stays lavish while the feeling gets conspicuously complicated.
sceneNote: The gold turns intimacy into set dressing. It looks like romance from across the room, which is exactly the point.
artFact: Klimt's geometric robe patterns contrast with the softer organic shapes of the couple's faces, making the embrace feel both ornamental and human.

sceneAlt: A soft blue-and-green scene study with floating lily pads and a small animal silhouette
artAlt: A study of Claude Monet's Water Lilies with blue water and green leaves
title: Water Lilies
museum: The National Museum of Western Art, Tokyo
choices: Franz Marc · The Blue Horse I
reveal: A pond of Monet-like color appears in the background, where a familiar floating motif becomes a running visual joke.
sceneNote: The reference makes the calm surface slightly suspicious. In BoJack's world, even a peaceful pond can be one bad decision away from a plot point.
artFact: Monet painted the pond at Giverny repeatedly, shifting from a readable landscape toward an almost abstract field of reflected light.

sceneNote: The allusion gives the room a pulse. The furniture is polished; the paintings keep the mess of a person in the frame.
artFact: Basquiat's crown is one of his recurring symbols: a quick, memorable mark that can read as royalty, self-invention, or pressure.

sceneAlt: A dark riverbank scene study with a floating figure and small bright flowers
artAlt: A study of John Everett Millais's Ophelia with a figure floating among flowers
title: Ophelia
choices: Sandro Botticelli · The Birth of Venus
reveal: Sarah Lynn's bedroom places a famous floating figure above the bed, a beautiful warning hiding in plain sight.
sceneNote: The composition is serene enough to make the danger easy to miss. That mismatch is the show's sharpest kind of foreshadowing.
artFact: Millais painted the flowers from life and staged Ophelia's pose in a bathtub, asking the model to remain still for long stretches.

sceneAlt: A seashell scene study with a small elephant figure and coral-pink sky
artAlt: A study of Sandro Botticelli's The Birth of Venus with a shell and wind lines
title: The Birth of Venus
choices: Sandro Botticelli · The Birth of Venus
reveal: At Elefante, Botticelli's shell-born Venus becomes a coy elephant tableau with Renaissance drama still intact.
sceneNote: The joke is immediate, but the staging is reverent: the parody keeps the wind, the shell, and the theatrical entrance.
artFact: Venus arrives on the shore after being born from sea foam; Botticelli's elongated proportions make the scene feel more poetic than anatomical.
